## Week 3 {.center}

### Q2 in depth: from population to analytic cohort

**A cohort is the first result of an analysis.**

Today we follow one study from a Methods paragraph to a dataset that can be analysed.

::: {.notes}
(2 min) TIMING: per-slide markers now sum to more than a single 150-minute slot, because
five slides were restored from the previous version. Treat the markers as relative
weights and select: the appendix slides, "Reviewing someone else's eligibility" and the
covariates preview are the first to drop. The audience knows epidemiology but may be new
to NHANES and data implementation.
Define every acronym when it first appears. Keep the focus on decisions and consequences,
not on memorising variable names.
:::

## Q2, in depth — and this week's division of labour

Week 2 gave you six questions. **Today is Q2:** who is the population, and how is
eligibility operationalised?

| | What it teaches | On which paper |
|---|---|---|
| **Tuesday (today)** | the **judgment** — turning a prose eligibility paragraph into logic you can defend | MASLD (Kueh) |
| **Thursday (L2)** | the **mechanics** — multi-cycle download, mortality linkage, eligibility steps, analytic dataset | benzodiazepine / opioid |
| **P1** | both, transferred | your locked paper |

- Framing question: *"If two teams read the same methods paragraph, would they build the
  same cohort?"*

> Eligibility decisions are analysis choices. That is why they sit inside Q2, not in a
> housekeeping appendix.

::: {.notes}
(4 min) Put the framing question to the room and take two answers before moving on. Most
will say "yes, obviously" — the alcohol slide proves otherwise, and that is the hinge of
the lecture. The table is the other load-bearing part: say out loud that Thursday's lab is
a *different paper on purpose*, so nobody spends the week thinking the course lost its
thread. We come back to it at the end with the actual code.
:::

## What you should be able to do by the end

Given a published Methods section, you should be able to:

1. identify the files and variables needed to build the cohort
2. translate each inclusion rule into executable logic
3. classify every reduction in N by its cause
4. document ambiguities and show what alternative decisions would change

**The standard is a defensible audit trail, not an unexplained match to the paper.**

::: {.notes}
(4 min) Connect to Week 2: target, source and analytic populations. Thursday's L2 repeats
the mechanics using a different paper. P1 transfers both the judgment and the mechanics
to the students' locked paper.
:::

## The complete cohort-building sequence

| Step | Question |
|---:|---|
| 0 | Which cycles, files and variables are needed? |
| 1 | Who meets the age rule? |
| 2 | Who has a computable Fatty Liver Index? |
| 3 | Who meets the metabolic dysfunction definition? |
| 4 | How is the alcohol exclusion implemented? |
| 5 | How are the four BMI and waist phenotypes defined? |
| 6 | How are covariates constructed? |
| 7–8 | How are mortality data linked, checked and saved? |

::: {.notes}
(4 min) This slide is the map. Return to it at each section change. Students should know
where they are in the sequence even when the variable details become unfamiliar.
:::

## Target, source, analytic — and what each step costs

| Population | Here | Why it narrows |
|---|---|---|
| **Target** | adults with MASLD in the US | who we want to speak about |
| **Source** | NHANES 2007–2018 respondents | who was sampled |
| **Analytic** | survivors of every filter, with exposure *and* outcome measurable | who we can compute on |

- Each narrowing step trades **generalizability** for **measurability**
- A drop is not automatically a bias. **What it is depends on its kind** — Week 2's five
  types, of which **only one is a missing-data problem**


::: {.notes}
(6 min) SAY THIS, it is the evidence for the arrow labels: Week 2's measured check found
adults in and out of the fasting subsample differ by 0.2 years, 0.02 kg/m2 and 0.07 cm.
Assignment to the subsample is design-based; fasting compliance can still add
nonresponse, which the subsample weight is there to address. Draw the nested circles if
you like, but the labels on the arrows matter more than the circles. Be careful here: an earlier version of this course taught every drop as a
preview of selection bias, and that was wrong — the measured balance in the blockquote is
why. The transferable habit is that the *kind* of each drop was checked rather than
assumed. We put the real typed funnel on screen after the break.
:::

# Part 1: From NHANES files to people

## A five-minute NHANES mental model

**Cycle**  
One two-year survey wave, such as 2011–2012

**Component**  
A topic-specific file, such as demographics, body measurements or laboratory tests

**Variable**  
A column inside a component, such as age or waist circumference

**`SEQN`**  
The participant identifier used to join files

This reproduction combines six cycles from 2007–2008 through 2017–2018.

::: {.notes}
(5 min) Students need only these four terms for the rest of the lecture. Cycle suffixes
E through J belong in the appendix, not in working memory. Point out that a participant
appears in several component files but has one SEQN.
:::

## Stack cycles first, then join components

For each component:

1. read the same variables from all six cycles
2. stack the cycles into one long file
3. join components by `SEQN`

```r
demo_all <- bind_rows(demo_E, demo_F, demo_G, demo_H, demo_I, demo_J)
dat <- left_join(demo_all, bmx_all, by = "SEQN")
```

**The join choice defines which people can remain in the analysis.**

::: {.notes}
(5 min) Connect to Week 2, where `full_join` vs `inner_join` was contrasted ("`inner_join`
would be a different study"), and to L1, where students implemented that merge. The
new complication is cycle availability: a column can be absent from a whole cycle. The
stacking helper pads absent variables with NA so the files can be combined.
:::

## An absent variable can look like nonresponse

Padding an unavailable variable with `NA` allows the code to run, but two situations then
look identical:

- the question did not exist in that cycle
- the question existed and the participant has no value

Example: `RIDRETH3`, which identifies non-Hispanic Asian participants, begins in
2011–2012. Earlier cycles cannot supply the same classification.

**Check variable availability by cycle before interpreting an `NA`.**

::: {.notes}
(5 min) This is the first major NHANES lesson. Connect to P1: the variable map must record
component, cycle availability, codes and transformations. Do not ask students to memorise
the variable code. Ask what the missingness means.
:::

# Part 2: Eligibility as executable logic

## The age sentence leaves a real decision

The paper states:

> “The study inclusion criteria were participants aged >18 years with evidence of MASLD.”

The reproduction uses:

```r
filter(age >= 18)
```

Because NHANES age is recorded in whole years:

- `age > 18` means age 19 and older
- `age >= 18` includes people aged exactly 18

::: {.notes}
(5 min) MASLD means metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. Ask the
room which rule they would use before showing the sensitivity results. The point is not
to guess the authors' intent. The point is to expose and test the decision.
:::

## The age sensitivity gives conflicting evidence

| Rule | Final N | Deaths | Mean age, SD |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Published paper | 6,300 | 585 | 51.0, 16.6 |
| Reproduction with age ≥18 | 6,371 | 586 | **51.0, 16.6** |
| Reproduction with age >18 | **6,301** | **585** | 51.4, 16.3 |

Seventy reproduced participants are exactly 18 years old.

<small>All reproduction rows are the **full reconstruction** row set (not the fasting-weight domain).</small>

**The strict rule matches N and deaths. The inclusive rule matches the age distribution.**

::: {.notes}
(7 min) This is the cleanest example of conflicting validation targets. Do not present
one rule as settled. A defensible report names the ambiguity and shows both analyses.
These counts come from the reproduction pipeline; the paper supplies the published row.
:::


## Exclusions are scientific claims

- Every filter answers *"who is this study about?"* — so every filter needs a **stated
  rationale**, not just a line of code
- The reproducibility contract, in one rule:

```r
# Paper, Methods: eligibility stated as "aged > 18 years"
d <- filter(d, age >= 18)     # NOT what the sentence says — deliberate, and recorded
```

- A comment naming **the sentence you are implementing** lets an auditor trace every
  `filter()` back to the paper, and makes a **divergence visible instead of invisible**

::: {.notes}
(5 min) Reframe "exclusion criteria" from a chore list into a set of claims. The age rule
is the smallest possible worked example of the comment rule: the sentence and the code
disagree, and the comment is what makes that checkable. Do not let anyone leave thinking
`>= 18` is a typo - it is a choice we wrote down. The next slide shows the three rules.
:::

## Same variable, three studies

Week 2 put **three** age rules on one slide:

| Study | Rule | Means |
|---|---|---|
| Thursday's lab (L2) | `>= 20` | 20 and over |
| This paper, as printed | `> 18` | 19 and over |
| Our reproduction | `>= 18` | 18 and over |

NHANES age is an integer, so one variable yields three different studies.

> The discipline is not to pick the right one. It is to **record which one you used**, so
> a reader can undo it. A reproduction that quietly adopts a different rule has destroyed
> its own evidence.

::: {.notes}
(3 min) Split from the previous slide so the comment rule and the three-rule comparison
each get room. Ask which they would defend. There is no single right answer, which is the
point - the alcohol criterion later is the same situation with no resolution available.
:::

# Part 3: Turning MASLD into data

## The paper constructs MASLD from measurements

In this study, a participant must have:

1. **hepatic steatosis**, defined using a Fatty Liver Index (FLI) of at least 60
2. **metabolic dysfunction**, defined by at least one of five criteria

NHANES does not provide one MASLD diagnosis column for these six cycles. The analyst
constructs the case definition.

2017–2018 includes liver transient elastography, but no comparable liver-imaging measure
spans all six cycles used by this paper.

::: {.notes}
(4 min) Avoid saying that NHANES has no liver imaging. It does in later cycles. The
problem is comparability across 2007–2018. Source for 2017–2018 imaging: CDC LUX_J
documentation. The paper chose FLI for a harmonised six-cycle definition.
:::

## The Fatty Liver Index uses four inputs

$$
\mathrm{FLI}=100\frac{\exp(L)}{1+\exp(L)}
$$

$$
L=0.953\ln(TG)+0.139(BMI)+0.718\ln(GGT)+0.053(waist)-15.745
$$

| Input | NHANES variable | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| Triglycerides (TG) | `LBXTR` | mg/dL |
| Body mass index (BMI) | `BMXBMI` | kg/m² |
| Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) | `LBXSGTSI` | U/L |
| Waist circumference | `BMXWAIST` | cm |

::: {.notes}
(6 min) Check the units before calculating. The formula uses natural logarithms for TG
and GGT. BMI and waist also help define the later exposure groups, which creates the
structural-dependence question examined in M1.
:::

## One participant can sit on either side of the FLI threshold

Hold BMI at 28.5 kg/m², GGT at 30 U/L and waist at 99 cm:

| Triglycerides | FLI | Steatosis by this rule? |
|---:|---:|:---:|
| 150 mg/dL | 66.4 | Yes |
| 110 mg/dL | 59.5 | No |

The cut occurs at approximately **112.4 mg/dL** for this profile.

**A continuous score becomes a hard inclusion boundary.**

::: {.notes}
(6 min) This is a hypothetical sensitivity demonstration, not a claim about within-person
triglyceride variability. Ask students what changes at the boundary: the measurements do
not become categorically different, but cohort membership does.
:::

## Fasting design and item missingness are different

Triglycerides come from a fasting laboratory subsample with its own weight, `WTSAF2YR`.

| Stage after age eligibility | N | Meaning |
|---|---:|---|
| Positive fasting subsample weight | 14,962 | Design-valid fasting domain |
| All four FLI inputs available | 14,170 | 792 additional records lack an input |

Assignment to the fasting subsample is design-based. Participation, fasting compliance
and laboratory nonresponse can still affect who has a positive weight and complete data.

::: {.notes}
(6 min) CDC states that the fasting weight applies to participants sampled to fast who
actually fasted for the required duration. Do not say that everyone without a positive
weight was never asked to fast. Connect the design restriction to P4 and the 792 missing
inputs to P5.
:::

## Two analytic row sets answer different questions

| | Full reconstruction | Fasting-weight domain |
|---|---:|---:|
| FLI computable | 14,989 | 14,170 |
| Final mortality-linked N | **6,371** | **6,048** |
| Main use | Reproduce the paper-like analysis | Design-aware population analysis |

The 323-person difference is not an arithmetic error.

**Every reported N should name its row set.**

::: {.notes}
(5 min) The paper does not report applying weights, strata or primary sampling units.
The full reconstruction best reproduces its tables. The 6,048-person domain is the
appropriate starting point when using the fasting subsample weight in P4.
:::

## Metabolic dysfunction requires at least one of five criteria

| Criterion | Operational rule |
|---|---|
| Adiposity | BMI ≥25, or waist >94 cm in men or >80 cm in women |
| Glycaemia | glucose ≥100, HbA1c ≥5.7%, diabetes diagnosis or treatment |
| Blood pressure | SBP ≥130, DBP ≥85 or treatment |
| Triglycerides | TG ≥150 or lipid-lowering treatment |
| HDL cholesterol | ≤40 in men or <50 in women |

The paper also mentions treatment targeting HDL. The supplied implementation has no
separate variable for that clause.

::: {.notes}
(8 min) SBP means systolic blood pressure; DBP means diastolic blood pressure; HDL means
high-density lipoprotein cholesterol. Five criteria must remain five indicators in code.
The code uses 100 mg/dL as the conventional equivalent of 5.6 mmol/L. A sensitivity cut
at 100.9 mg/dL changes no final classifications.
:::

## Two participants meet none of the five criteria

Both have FLI-defined steatosis, but no operational cardiometabolic criterion:

| SEQN | BMI, waist | Glucose, HbA1c | BP | TG, HDL |
|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 58194 | 22.2, 87.2 cm | 94, 5.6% | 120/67 | 108, 141 |
| 71217 | 24.9, 93.3 cm | 99, 5.0% | 109/62 | 135, 47 |

Therefore, the MASLD step changes **6,376 to 6,374** in the full reconstruction.

An unresolved criterion contributes no positive count. Check whether each `NA` is a
structural skip, cycle absence, refusal or genuine missingness before interpreting it.

::: {.notes}
(6 min) These are the two people excluded by the MASLD criterion, not the two people lost
at mortality linkage in the fasting-weight funnel. SEQN 58194 is age 46 in 2009–2010;
SEQN 71217 is age 28 in 2011–2012. Say “none of the five operational criteria,” not “no
metabolic abnormality.”
:::

# Part 4: A Methods sentence can produce several cohorts

## The alcohol sentence is not executable as written

The paper excludes consumption above two drinks per day for men and one for women.

The sentence leaves three questions:

- Does “per day” mean per drinking day or an average over all days?
- Which variables supply frequency and quantity?
- What should happen when an alcohol response is missing?

`ALQ130` records drinks **on drinking days**, not average drinks per calendar day.

::: {.notes}
(5 min) Ask the class to propose code before showing the alternatives. Three drinks every
Saturday means ALQ130 equals 3, but average consumption is about 0.4 drinks per day.
:::

## Three implementations produce three cohorts

| Implementation | Removed | Final N |
|---|---:|---:|
| Threshold `ALQ130` directly | 2,063 | 4,308 |
| Frequency × quantity averaged per day | 427 | 5,944 |
| Alcohol exclusion switched off | 0 | **6,371** |
| Published paper |  | **6,300** |

<small>Counts are the **full reconstruction** row set.</small>

Among the tested alcohol implementations, switching the exclusion off comes closest to
the published cohort. It does not prove what the authors implemented.

The age >18 sensitivity, not the alcohol rule, explains most of the remaining 71-person gap.

::: {.notes}
(8 min) Keep the conclusion cautious. The paper does not publish operational code for
alcohol. The frequency-weighted rule is plausible, but missing responses are set to zero
in the supplied implementation, so it remains a documented analytic choice.
:::

## Reserved codes can look like extreme measurements

For `ALQ130`:

| Code | Meaning |
|---:|---|
| 777 | Refused |
| 999 | Do not know |

```r
qty <- ifelse(ALQ130 %in% c(777, 999), NA, ALQ130)
```

Leaving these codes in reclassifies nine refusals as extremely heavy drinkers.

**Missing-value codes are variable-specific. Always check the codebook.**

::: {.notes}
(5 min) Contrast with a laboratory value: triglycerides of 77 mg/dL are real. There is
no global NHANES rule that 7, 77 or 777 always means missing.
:::

## The analysis switch records the decision

```r
APPLY_ALCOHOL_EXCL <- FALSE
```

The pipeline still:

- constructs the alcohol variable
- saves the heavy-drinking flag
- reports the alternative cohort size
- writes the switch setting into the funnel

**A visible switch preserves the unresolved question for the next analyst.**

::: {.notes}
(4 min) This is better than silently deleting the exclusion or quietly changing its
meaning. Connect to P1: one ambiguous sentence, the chosen implementation, the reason and
the alternative consequence belong in the student's decision ledger.
:::

## BREAK {.center}

### Restart question

Which alcohol implementation would you defend, and what would you write in the Methods?

::: {.notes}
(10 min) Leave this prompt visible. Invite two different defensible answers after the
break. The learning objective is transparent justification, not unanimity.
:::

# Part 5: Exposure, covariates and outcome

## The exposure has four BMI and waist phenotypes

Obesity means BMI ≥30 kg/m², or ≥25 kg/m² for Asian participants. High central adiposity
means waist-to-height ratio (WHtR) ≥0.6.

| | WHtR <0.6 | WHtR ≥0.6 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Obesity | Group I: 391 | Group II: 4,585 |
| No obesity | Group III: 787 | Group IV: 608 |

The exposure shares BMI and waist inputs with FLI. M1 asks what that structural dependence
does to interpretation.

::: {.notes}
(6 min) WHtR equals waist circumference divided by height, both in centimetres. The group
counts use the full 6,371-person reconstruction. Group I is the reference group in the
paper's Cox models; it is not a “healthy” or unexposed population.
:::

## Asian status is unavailable in the first two cycles

`RIDRETH3` supplies a separate non-Hispanic Asian category only from 2011–2012 onward.

In 2007–2010:

- the available race variable combines “other race” and multiracial participants
- Asian participants cannot be isolated reliably
- the supplied code treats missing Asian status as “not Asian”

Seventeen early-cycle participants lie in the BMI range where Asian status could change
their phenotype. **Seventeen is an upper bound, not a known error count.**

::: {.notes}
(5 min) This is the payoff from the earlier cycle-availability slide. The general rule is
not “drop early cycles.” It is “state what the data cannot identify, bound the possible
consequence, and test sensitivity when possible.”
:::

## The paper's BMI labels conflict with its Methods

**Methods:** obesity uses BMI ≥30 kg/m², with the Asian-specific cut at 25.

**Table headers:** groups are labelled BMI ≥25 and BMI <25.

**Published non-obesity medians:** 27.6 and 28.8 kg/m².

Those medians cannot belong to groups defined entirely by BMI <25. Coding the general cut
at 30 reproduces all four published group medians.

**The table labels appear to be wrong; the Methods and reproduced distributions agree.**

::: {.notes}
(5 min) Connect to M2: use internal evidence to adjudicate a discrepancy, but avoid claims
about author intent. Contrast with the age rule, where different published statistics
support different interpretations and the ambiguity remains unresolved.
:::

## Cohort construction exposes under-specified covariates

The paper says that comorbidity definitions were “previously described,” without giving
the full operational rules in this article.

The reproduction must choose definitions for hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidaemia,
chronic kidney disease and medication use.

**Do not choose a definition because it makes Table 1 match.** Record the rule first, then
report the residual difference.

This problem returns in **P2**, when Table 1 and confounding variables are constructed.

::: {.notes}
(5 min) The supplied code comments say some composites were calibrated to published
prevalences. Treat that as a disclosed limitation, not a model for good practice. The
full technical definitions belong in the appendix or P2 lecture.
:::

## Mortality comes from a separate linked file

The NCHS linked mortality files supply:

- mortality status
- underlying cause category
- follow-up time through 31 December 2019

The reproduction uses `PERMTH_EXM`, months from the mobile examination centre visit,
because BMI and waist were measured at that examination.

The paper does not state whether it used examination-based or interview-based follow-up.

::: {.notes}
(6 min) NCHS means National Center for Health Statistics. Connect to L2, which uses
`PERMTH_INT` in one eligibility rule. Time zero should align with when the exposure was
measured. Mention, without dwelling on it, that the saved `cv_death` variable combines
heart and cerebrovascular causes while the Table 2 reproduction uses heart-only deaths.
:::

# Part 6: The funnel is an analytic result

## The fasting-weight funnel names the cause of every reduction

| Step | Criterion | N | Kind |
|---:|---|---:|---|
| 0 | NHANES 2007–2018 | 59,842 | Source frame |
| 1 | Age ≥18 | 36,580 | Eligibility |
| 2 | Positive fasting weight | 14,962 | Design domain |
| 3 | FLI computable | 14,170 | Item missingness |
| 4 | FLI ≥60 | 6,052 | Target population |
| 5 | At least one criterion | 6,050 | Target population |
| 6 | Phenotype assigned | 6,050 | Classification check |
| 7 | Mortality linked | **6,048** | Outcome ascertainment |

::: {.notes}
(8 min) Walk the kind column rather than the N column. The two people lost at mortality
linkage here are not the two people excluded by the MASLD criterion. A funnel reports who
left and why; those reasons determine whether the response belongs to P4, P5 or the study
population definition.
:::

## The full reconstruction follows a different path

| Stage | N |
|---|---:|
| Age ≥18 | 36,580 |
| FLI computable | 14,989 |
| FLI ≥60 | 6,376 |
| At least one criterion | 6,374 |
| Phenotype assigned | 6,374 |
| Mortality linked | **6,371** |

This path best reproduces the paper's ordinary analyses. It fuses fasting design and data
availability at the FLI step, so it should not replace the design-aware funnel.

::: {.notes}
(5 min) The paper reports N=6,300. The reproduction has 6,371. The purpose of this slide
is not to call 6,371 correct. It is to show which sequence produces the analysis file
used for the reproduced tables and figures.
:::


## Why you never tune the cohort to hit the paper's N

- The temptation: quietly flip a threshold until N matches the abstract
- That is **fitting the process to the answer** — you have chosen your method using the
  result, and the method no longer carries evidence
- One sentence in this paper moves N by **2,063**. So an exact match is roughly as likely
  to mean *you guessed their ambiguity correctly* as *you implemented it correctly*

| | What it demonstrates |
|---|---|
| Matched N, undocumented coding | nothing — the match is unattributable |
| Mismatched N, traced to a named step | the reproduction worked |

> A documented N you can defend beats a matched N you cannot.

::: {.notes}
(7 min) The methodological heart of the reproduction philosophy, and it follows directly
from the alcohol slide rather than being asserted. Reframe success explicitly: at M1, a
gap you can trace to a specific decision scores above a match you cannot explain. The
grading criteria say so.
:::

## A short decisions ledger preserves the audit trail

| Decision or limitation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Age ≥18 versus >18 | 70 participants; different published targets match |
| Alcohol exclusion switched off | 427 would leave under the frequency-weighted rule |
| Asian status unavailable in early cycles | At most 17 phenotype assignments could change |
| Full versus fasting-weight row set | 6,371 versus 6,048 |
| Examination versus interview clock | Paper does not specify the choice |

**A decision without a quantified consequence is not fully documented.**

::: {.notes}
(5 min) Ask students to classify the rows: ambiguity, data limitation, analysis setting
or outcome definition. This becomes material for the limitations section rather than a
private coding note.
:::

# Part 7: Transfer to the rest of the course

## Thursday's L2 builds the same object from another paper

The benzodiazepine, opioid and mortality lab repeats the same mechanics:

```r
dat.mort   <- rbind(mortality_cycles)
dat.nhanes <- rbind(nhanes_cycles)
dat <- merge(dat.mort, dat.nhanes, by = "SEQN", all = TRUE)
```

Then it applies a numbered chain of eligibility rules.

**Your task in L2:** write N remaining, N removed and the reason for every step.

> If you can only do it on MASLD, you have not learned it.

::: {.notes}
(6 min) Connect `all=TRUE` to Week 2's `full_join`. The lab is intentionally a different
paper. Transfer across papers is evidence that students learned a method rather than one
set of MASLD variable names.
:::


## One more thing to notice on Thursday

L2's exposure has four levels, and the reference category is **"Neither"**:

```r
dat6 <- subset(dat5, benzodiazepines == "Yes" | ssris == "Yes" | opioids == "Yes")
dat6$exposure <- relevel(dat6$exposure, ref = "Neither")
```

- Eligibility required **at least one** of three drug classes. So "Neither" means *neither
  benzodiazepines nor opioids* — **everyone in it is an SSRI user**
- The reference group is an **active comparator**, not an unexposed population
- Exactly the shape of our Group I: every hazard ratio in the MASLD paper is measured
  against a group that is **obese**

> A ratio without its referent means nothing — and in both studies the referent is not
> "healthy".

::: {.notes}
(4 min) This is the best transfer point in the two studies and it is easy to miss in the
lab, so plant it now. The eligibility rule and the reference category are the *same
decision* seen twice: who you let into the cohort determines what your comparison can
mean. Week 2 made this point about Group I; here it is again in a completely different
paper, which is the evidence that it is a general property rather than a quirk.
:::

## The same cohort work returns in P1 through P5

| Increment | What this lecture contributes |
|---|---|
| P1 | Cohort code, decision ledger and typed funnel |
| P2 | Operational covariates and Table 1 |
| P3 | An interaction analysis not present in this reproduction |
| P4 | Fasting subsample weight, strata and primary sampling units |
| P5 | The 792 missing FLI inputs and later complete-case losses |

M1 asks which threat matters most. M2 asks what reproduced and what did not. M3 asks you
to defend the decisions person by person.

::: {.notes}
(6 min) Do not imply that this pipeline already completes P3. It does not. P3 is the
student's extension. P4 uses the 6,048-person fasting-weight mortality-linked domain.
P5 addresses genuine missingness, not the deliberate fasting-domain restriction.
:::

## What to take into P1

For each cohort step, write four lines:

1. **Paper:** the exact statement or definition
2. **Problem:** the ambiguity or data limitation
3. **Decision:** the implemented rule and rationale
4. **Consequence:** the change in N, classification or estimate

Then label the consequence: eligibility, design, item missingness, target population or
outcome ascertainment.

> Be ready to show one person who enters or leaves because of your decision.

::: {.notes}
(4 min) Close by asking students to identify one sentence in their locked paper that may
not survive translation into code. Remind them that P1 is the reusable foundation for
later increments, not a disposable data-cleaning exercise.
:::

## Appendix: And L2 writes a funnel — it just does not know it yet {visibility="uncounted"}

```r
dat1 <- subset(dat,  RIDAGEYR >= 20)                            # N = 43,793
dat2 <- subset(dat1, RIDSTATR == "int + mec exam")              # N = 41,659
dat3 <- subset(dat2, TAKERX_INLASTMONTH %in% c("No", "Yes"))    # N = 41,614
dat4 <- dat3[complete.cases(dat3$BPQ020), ]                     # N not recorded
dat5 <- subset(dat4, mortstat == 0 | (mortstat == 1 & permth_int > 12))  # N = 31,591
dat6 <- subset(dat5, benzodiazepines == "Yes" | ssris == "Yes" | opioids == "Yes")  # N = 4,049
```

- Six eligibility steps, **N after each one** — that is a funnel, written as comments
- Now type it, the way we typed ours:

| | `dat1` | `dat2` | `dat3` | `dat4` | `dat5` | `dat6` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| kind | `ELIGIBILITY` | `DESIGN` | `MISSINGNESS` | `MISSINGNESS` | `ELIGIBILITY` | `TARGET POPULATION` |

- **`dat4` prints no N.** The complete-case steps are the ones that go uncounted — in this
  lab and in most papers

::: {.notes}
(7 min) The payoff slide for the whole lecture. They are looking at a real funnel in the
wild, in the crudest possible form: a numbered chain with N in comments. Ask the room to
supply the type row before you reveal it — arguing about whether `dat2` is design or
missingness is exactly the right argument. Then point at `dat4`: the step with no number is
the complete-case step, which is the one most likely to be doing quiet work. That is the
habit P1 is testing.
:::

## Appendix: Reviewing someone else's eligibility {visibility="uncounted"}

| Ask | On this paper |
|---|---|
| Is the case definition **operational**? | mostly — FLI ≥ 60 is exact; "≥ 1 criterion" needs the five spelled out |
| Is every exclusion **executable** as written? | **no** — the alcohol criterion is not |
| Does the funnel's arithmetic **close**? | not reported; we had to rebuild it |
| Is the analytic N **stated and reproducible**? | stated; reproducible only up to the above |

- Also check the tables against the Methods: here the Table 1–2 headers read **"BMI < 25"**
  while the Methods define obesity at **≥ 30**, and the non-obese groups have BMI medians
  of **27.6** and **28.8** — so the headers appear to be a labelling error
- **Charity and rigour together:** assume competence, and still require that the numbers
  reconcile

::: {.notes}
(6 min) This is the stance they bring to M2 and to their own defence at M3. The BMI header
is the cleanest small example in the course of a typographic slip with real consequences —
a reproducer who codes to 25 does not reproduce the groups. Note the hedge "appear to be":
we report what we can check, and we do not diagnose intent.
:::
